title: Sets, subsets, and complements
terms: set; element; membership; set-builder notation; family of sets; empty set; subset; proper subset; superset; universal set; complement; relative complement; set difference.

exposition.text:
A set is determined by its elements, with x ∈ A denoting membership. Set-builder notation {x :
P(x)} describes elements satisfying a property. The empty set has no elements. The assertion
A ⊆ B means every element of A belongs to B; a proper subset additionally differs from B.
Equality can be proved by the two inclusions.
c
Relative to a fixed universe U, the complement is A = U \ A; the difference A \ B consists
of elements in A but not B. Membership and inclusion are different: ∅ ⊆ A always, but ∅ ∈
A only when the empty set is itself a listed element. A family of sets is simply a set whose
members are sets.
The notation B ⊇ A says that B is a superset of A, equivalently A ⊆ B. We write A ⊊ B for
strict inclusion. A universal set fixes which objects are under discussion; changing it can change
the complement even when A stays the same. A set ignores repetition and the order in which
its members are listed.

question.text:
Let A = {∅, {∅}}. How many members of A are also subsets of A?
(A) 0 (B) 1 (C) 2 (D) 3 (E) 4

solution.text:
The member ∅ is a subset of every set. The other member {∅} is also a subset of A
because its sole element ∅ belongs to A. Thus both members qualify.

question.text:
For arbitrary sets A, B, C with A ⊆ B, which statement must be true?
(A) C \ A ⊆ C \ B (B) C \ B ⊆ C \ A (C) A \ C = B \ C (D) B \ A = ∅ (E) A ∈ B

solution.text:
An element of C \ B lies in C and not in B. Since A ⊆ B, it cannot lie in A, so it lies in C \
A. Taking complements reverses inclusion.

question.text:
A set A has five elements and B ⊂ A has two elements. How many subsets of A contain B?
(A) 10 (B) 32 (C) 16 (D) 4 (E) 8

solution.text:
The two elements of B are compulsory. Each of the remaining three elements can be
3
included or excluded independently, giving 2 = 8 subsets.

question.text:
If A ⊆ B and B ⊆ C, which identity must hold?
(A) C ⊆ B (B) A = C (C) A ∩ C = A (D) A ∪ C = A (E) B \ A = ∅

solution.text:
Transitivity gives A ⊆ C, so intersecting A with C leaves exactly A. The inclusions need
not be equalities.
